Depression sender and receiver effects were substantively negligible across all schools; although the sender effect in School B reached statistical significance across model specifications owing to very small standard errors, its magnitude (AME < 0.001) indicates no meaningful association, and AI identity was largely unassociated with sending or receiving ties, with only a borderline positive receiver effect in School C.

Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools, indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation. Sexual orientation homophily was also significant and positive.

Most notably, School C was the only setting where incoming ties were significantly centralized (negative GWIDeg), indicating a pronounced popularity hierarchy in which a small subset of students received disproportionately many nominations.
Reciprocity was positive and highly significant in every model, indicating a robust tendency for mutual friendship nominations.

Similarly, the positive coefficients for closed triads (transitivity) and negative coefficients for two‑path confirmed that triadic closure—the process by which friends of friends become friends—is a fundamental organizing principle within these AI adolescent networks.

The negative and significant coefficients for geometrically weighted outdegree (GWODeg) across all schools indicate a centralized structure in outgoing ties, meaning a subset of adolescents initiated a disproportionately high number of friendship nominations.

For incoming ties (indegree), a significant negative coefficient was observed only in School C, indicating a centralized popularity structure in that setting. In Schools A and B, indegree distributions did not deviate significantly from what would be expected by chance.
Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.

More importantly, cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time [4,18,48].

Accordingly, the results reported here should be interpreted as associations between actor attributes and friendship tie formation, not as evidence that substance use, depression, or AI identity causally affect friendship formation, nor as evidence that friendship networks causally shape these attributes.

Furthermore, we acknowledge that these data reflect only one developmental epoch of adolescents at one time point. Relational patterns among AI youth will likely differ across the life course, especially in the formative adolescent years that are not captured here.

The literature highlights the role that school transitions (elementary to middle to high school) play in adolescent networks, but our cross-sectional design imposes a fundamental interpretive limit: a single, simultaneous observation of the network and of individual attributes cannot capture changes in network formation and behavior over time.
Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.

Lastly, as reservations are sovereign nations and have policies and laws that may differ from the rest of the state, we encourage future research to explore the role of local governance around these issues and the implications they might have on adolescent social network formation and related interventions.
Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.

By focusing on reservation schools, where AI youth are the norm rather than a statistical minority, this research moves beyond generalizations derived from prior research and contributes new insights into the unique architecture of AI adolescent social worlds.

These findings challenge assumptions underpinning many network-based prevention programs and underscore the critical need for theories and interventions that are culturally and contextually grounded in the lived experiences of AI youth.
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.
This paper takes an initial step toward understanding these dynamics by investigating the role of substance use in the formation of friendship ties within AI‑majority schools.

This study addresses this gap by collecting and analyzing first-hand social network data from 9th- and 10th-grade students in three schools on a Northern Plains reservation. Using exponential random graph models (ERGMs) [9,23], we examine how demographic attributes, substance use behaviors, depression, and AI identity are associated with friendship formation within these AI-majority educational contexts.

In racially heterogeneous schools, substance use—alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana—consistently predicts friendship dynamics. Adolescents who use substances tend to receive more friendship nominations (positive receiver effects) [13], and homophily on substance use is well documented: youth are more likely to befriend peers with similar consumption patterns [11,22].
These patterns reflect a social ecology in which risky behaviors confer status and serve as a basis for peer identification in diverse, often anonymizing school environments [20].
Cultural frameworks emphasizing communal well-being, collective responsibility, and egalitarianism de-emphasize individual status competition [26,27].
Most existing research on adolescent networks derives from racially heterogeneous school settings, where substance use is often linked to friendship formation and popularity.

In non-AI samples, substance use homophily and receiver effects are consistently positive and often substantial in magnitude [6,11,13,22] (see Table 1 for a summary of prior findings). By contrast, in our AI-majority sample, substance use showed no consistent sender, receiver, or homophily effects across schools.
